As small as you can and still look as good as you need them to look.\n\n##  JPG vs PNG\n\nThis is pretty much the same as regular HTML in that JPGs have lossy compression, PNGs have lossless compression so PNGs are generally slower to download. But, PNGs support transparency. PNGs are also probably the appropriate format for non-image data like normal maps, and other kinds of non-image maps which we'll go over later.\n\nIt's important to remember that a JPG doesn't use less memory than a PNG in WebGL. See above.\n\n##  Filtering and Mips\n\nLet's apply this 16x16 texture\n\nTo a cube\n\nLet's draw that cube really small\n\nHmmm, I guess that's hard to see. Let's magnify that tiny cube\n\nHow does the GPU know which colors to make each pixel it's drawing for the tiny cube? What if the cube was so small that it's just 1 or 2 pixels?\n\nThis is what filtering is about.\n\nIf it was Photoshop, Photoshop would average nearly all the pixels together to figure out what color to make those 1 or 2 pixels. That would be a very slow operation. GPUs solve this issue using mipmaps.\n\nMips are copies of the texture, each one half as wide and half as tall as the previous mip where the pixels have been blended to make the next smaller mip. Mips are created until we get all the way to a 1x1 pixel mip. For the image above all of the mips would end up being something like this\n\nNow, when the cube is drawn so small that it's only 1 or 2 pixels large the GPU can choose to use just the smallest or next to smallest mip level to decide what color to make the tiny cube.\n\nIn three.js you can choose what happens both when the texture is drawn larger than its original size and what happens when it's drawn smaller than its original size.\n\nFor setting the filter when the texture is drawn larger than its original size you set texture.magFilter property to either &#96;THREE.NearestFilter&#96; or&#96;THREE.LinearFilter&#96;. &#96;NearestFilter&#96; means just pick the closet single pixel from the original texture. With a low resolution texture this gives you a very pixelated look like Minecraft.\n\n&#96;LinearFilter&#96; means choose the 4 pixels from the texture that are closest to the where we should be choosing a color from and blend them in the appropriate proportions relative to how far away the actual point is from each of the 4 pixels.\n\nNearest\n\nLinear\n\nFor setting the filter when the texture is drawn smaller than its original size you set the texture.minFilter property to one of 6 values.\n\n* &#96;THREE.NearestFilter&#96;  \n same as above, choose the closest pixel in the texture\n* &#96;THREE.LinearFilter&#96;  \n same as above, choose 4 pixels from the texture and blend them\n* &#96;THREE.NearestMipmapNearestFilter&#96;  \n choose the appropriate mip then choose one pixel\n* &#96;THREE.NearestMipmapLinearFilter&#96;  \n choose 2 mips, choose one pixel from each, blend the 2 pixels\n* &#96;THREE.LinearMipmapNearestFilter&#96;  \n chose the appropriate mip then choose 4 pixels and blend them\n* &#96;THREE.LinearMipmapLinearFilter&#96;  \nchoose 2 mips, choose 4 pixels from each and blend all 8 into 1 pixel\n\nHere's an example showing all 6 settings\n\nclick to  \nchange  \ntexture\n\nnearest\n\nlinear\n\nnearest  \nmipmap  \nnearest\n\nnearest  \nmipmap  \nlinear\n\nlinear  \nmipmap  \nnearest\n\nlinear  \nmipmap  \nlinear\n\nOne thing to notice is the top left and top middle using &#96;NearestFilter&#96; and &#96;LinearFilter&#96;don't use the mips. Because of that they flicker in the distance because the GPU is picking pixels from the original texture. On the left just one pixel is chosen and in the middle 4 are chosen and blended but it's not enough come up with a good representative color. The other 4 strips do better with the bottom right,&#96;LinearMipmapLinearFilter&#96; being best.\n\nIf you click the picture above it will toggle between the texture we've been using above and a texture where every mip level is a different color.\n\nThis makes it more clear what is happening. You can see in the top left and top middle the first mip is used all the way into the distance. The top right and bottom middle you can clearly see where a different mip is used.\n\nSwitching back to the original texture you can see the bottom right is the smoothest, highest quality. You might ask why not always use that mode. The most obvious reason is sometimes you want things to be pixelated for a retro look or some other reason. The next most common reason is that reading 8 pixels and blending them is slower than reading 1 pixel and blending. While it's unlikely that a single texture is going to be the difference between fast and slow as we progress further into these articles we'll eventually have materials that use 4 or 5 textures all at once. 4 textures \\* 8 pixels per texture is looking up 32 pixels for ever pixel rendered. This can be especially important to consider on mobile devices.\n\n##  Repeating, offseting, rotating, wrapping a texture\n\nTextures have settings for repeating, offseting, and rotating a texture.\n\nBy default textures in three.js do not repeat. To set whether or not a texture repeats there are 2 properties, wrapS for horizontal wrapping and wrapT for vertical wrapping.\n\nThey can be set to one of:\n\n* &#96;THREE.ClampToEdgeWrapping&#96;  \n the last pixel on each edge is repeated forever\n* &#96;THREE.RepeatWrapping&#96;  \n the texture is repeated\n* &#96;THREE.MirroredRepeatWrapping&#96;  \n the texture is mirrored and repeated\n\nFor example to turn on wrapping in both directions:\n\nsomeTexture.wrapS = THREE.RepeatWrapping;\nsomeTexture.wrapT = THREE.RepeatWrapping;\n\nRepeating is set with the \\[repeat\\] repeat property.\n\nconst timesToRepeatHorizontally = 4;\nconst timesToRepeatVertically = 2;\nsomeTexture.repeat.set(timesToRepeatHorizontally, timesToRepeatVertically);\n\nOffseting the texture can be done by setting the &#96;offset&#96; property. Textures are offset with units where 1 unit = 1 texture size. On other words 0 = no offset and 1 = offset one full texture amount.\n\nconst xOffset = .5;   // offset by half the texture\nconst yOffset = .25;  // offset by 1/4 the texture\nsomeTexture.offset.set(xOffset, yOffset);\n\nRotating the texture can be set by setting the &#96;rotation&#96; property in radians as well as the &#96;center&#96; property for choosing the center of rotation. It defaults to 0,0 which rotates from the bottom left corner. Like offset these units are in texture size so setting them to &#96;.5, .5&#96; would rotate around the center of the texture.\n\nsomeTexture.center.set(.5, .5);\nsomeTexture.rotation = THREE.MathUtils.degToRad(45);\n\nLet's modify the top sample above to play with these values\n\nFirst we'll keep a reference to the texture so we can manipulate it\n\n+const texture = loader.load('resources/images/wall.jpg');\nconst material = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({\n-  map: loader.load('resources/images/wall.jpg');\n+  map: texture,\n});\n\nThen we'll use lil-gui again to provide a simple interface.\n\nimport {GUI} from 'three/addons/libs/lil-gui.module.min.js';\n\nAs we did in previous lil-gui examples we'll use a simple class to give lil-gui an object that it can manipulate in degrees but that will set a property in radians.\n\nclass DegRadHelper {\n  constructor(obj, prop) {\n    this.obj = obj;\n    this.prop = prop;\n  }\n  get value() {\n    return THREE.MathUtils.radToDeg(this.obj[this.prop]);\n  }\n  set value(v) {\n    this.obj[this.prop] = THREE.MathUtils.degToRad(v);\n  }\n}\n\nWe also need a class that will convert from a string like &#96;\"123\"&#96; into a number like &#96;123&#96; since three.js requires numbers for enum settings like &#96;wrapS&#96; and &#96;wrapT&#96; but lil-gui only uses strings for enums.\n\nclass StringToNumberHelper {\n  constructor(obj, prop) {\n    this.obj = obj;\n    this.prop = prop;\n  }\n  get value() {\n    return this.obj[this.prop];\n  }\n  set value(v) {\n    this.obj[this.prop] = parseFloat(v);\n  }\n}\n\nUsing those classes we can setup a simple GUI for the settings above\n\nconst wrapModes = {\n  'ClampToEdgeWrapping': THREE.ClampToEdgeWrapping,\n  'RepeatWrapping': THREE.RepeatWrapping,\n  'MirroredRepeatWrapping': THREE.MirroredRepeatWrapping,\n};\n\nfunction updateTexture() {\n  texture.needsUpdate = true;\n}\n\nconst gui = new GUI();\ngui.add(new StringToNumberHelper(texture, 'wrapS'), 'value', wrapModes)\n  .name('texture.wrapS')\n  .onChange(updateTexture);\ngui.add(new StringToNumberHelper(texture, 'wrapT'), 'value', wrapModes)\n  .name('texture.wrapT')\n  .onChange(updateTexture);\ngui.add(texture.repeat, 'x', 0, 5, .01).name('texture.repeat.x');\ngui.add(texture.repeat, 'y', 0, 5, .01).name('texture.repeat.y');\ngui.add(texture.offset, 'x', -2, 2, .01).name('texture.offset.x');\ngui.add(texture.offset, 'y', -2, 2, .01).name('texture.offset.y');\ngui.add(texture.center, 'x', -.5, 1.5, .01).name('texture.center.x');\ngui.add(texture.center, 'y', -.5, 1.5, .01).name('texture.center.y');\ngui.add(new DegRadHelper(texture, 'rotation'), 'value', -360, 360)\n  .name('texture.rotation');\n\nThe last thing to note about the example is that if you change &#96;wrapS&#96; or&#96;wrapT&#96; on the texture you must also set texture.needsUpdateso three.js knows to apply those settings. The other settings are automatically applied.\n\nclick here to open in a separate window \n\nThis is only one step into the topic of textures. At some point we'll go over texture coordinates as well as 9 other types of textures that can be applied to materials.\n\nFor now let's move on to lights.",

      "chunk": "EnglishDeutsch日本語한국어Português BrasileiroРусский简体中文 Table of Contents \n\n# WebGL2Fundamentals.org\n\nFix, Fork, Contribute \n\n# Tex image TEXTURE\\_2D level 0 is incurring lazy initialization\n\n## Question:\n\nI got the error message: &#96;Error: WebGL warning: drawElements: Tex image TEXTURE_2D level 0 is incurring lazy initialization.&#96; on WebGL and I want to know what is actually means.\n\nHow is lazy initialization even a problem in a single-thread application anyway? I understand it as when you initialize a variable inside a getter?\n\nI tried looking for my error message didn’t really find any good info on it.\n\nThis is my code for handling textures:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n            const images = await Promise.all(model.maps.map(map =\u003e new Promise((resolve, reject) =\u003e {\n                const image = new Image();\n\n                image.src = map;\n                image.onload = event =\u003e {\n                    const texture = gl.createTexture();\n\n                    gl.bindTexture(gl.TEXTURE_2D, texture);\n                    gl.texImage2D(gl.TEXTURE_2D, 0, gl.RGBA, image.width, image.height, 0, gl.RGBA, gl.FLOAT, null);\n                    gl.texParameteri(gl.TEXTURE_2D, gl.TEXTURE_MAG_FILTER, gl.NEAREST);\n                    gl.texParameteri(gl.TEXTURE_2D, gl.TEXTURE_MIN_FILTER, gl.NEAREST);\n                    gl.texParameteri(gl.TEXTURE_2D, gl.TEXTURE_WRAP_S, gl.CLAMP_TO_EDGE);\n                    gl.texParameteri(gl.TEXTURE_2D, gl.TEXTURE_WRAP_T, gl.CLAMP_TO_EDGE);\n\n                    gl.bindTexture(gl.TEXTURE_2D, null);\n\n                    resolve(texture);\n                };\n\n                image.onerror = error =\u003e {\n                    console.log(error);\n                    resolve(null);\n                };\n            })));\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThe relevant part of my draw function is basically:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\ngl.bindTexture(gl.TEXTURE_2D, textures[material.textureIndex]);\ngl.activeTexture(gl.TEXTURE0);\ngl.drawElements(gl.TRIANGLES, material.faceCount * 3, gl.UNSIGNED_SHORT, drawnCount);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nWith that said, if I use the 6 argument syntax: &#96; gl.texImage2D(gl.TEXTURE_2D, 0, gl.RGBA, gl.RGBA, gl.FLOAT, image);&#96; then this error message no longer shows and I manage to render correctly.\n\n## Answer:\n\nIt’s not an error. It’s a warning.\n\n\u003e Error: WebGL **warning** …\n\nIt’s super confusing it says “Error” in front but even if it only said “warning” I’ve argued for a long time it’s bad warning.\n\nThe warning is that WebGL needed to do some non-trivial work.\n\nWhen you make a texture and you don’t pass it any data, you passed &#96;null&#96; as the last parameter to &#96;texImage2D&#96;, it means at some point WebGL has to clear the texture. Let’s say that texture is 2048x2048 RGBA/UNSIGNED\\_BYTE. Effectively WebGL has to allocate 16meg of ram (2048x2048x4), clear that 16meg of ram to 0, and call &#96;gl.texSubImage2D&#96; to put zeros in the texture just before the texture is actually used. If they didn’t do this the texture would have random data in it, data that might be secrets, passwords, previous graphics memory like photos, or whatever.\n\nSo, the warning is telling you some non-trivial work happened.\n\nThe problem with this warning is the workaround to stop the warning is worse than the warning itself. The workaround is for you to clear the texture yourself. To do that you’d need to allocate 16meg in JavaScript as in &#96;new Uint8Array(2048 * 2048 * 4)&#96;. That means JavaScript is allocating 16meg, it also clears that 16 meg. It also allocates a &#96;Uint8Array&#96; object to track that 16meg. That &#96;Uint8Array&#96; object is a complex JavaScript object, likely a collection of multiple objects composited together, for example an &#96;ArrayBuffer&#96; object is also allocated. The objects both have prototype chains and the ability to have properties and methods and getters and setters added to them. That &#96;Uint8Array&#96; and &#96;ArrayBuffer&#96; also have to be tracked so they can be garbage collected later meaning there is overhead in them even existing. Worse, if the browser is multi-process which Chrome is and I believe Firefox is working toward, then that 16meg allocated in JavaScript has to copied to the GPU process which means first the GPU process needs to allocate 16meg of ram as well, the data has to copied from the process running the webpage to the GPU process so it can be passed to the graphics driver. Even way more work.\n\nSo in other words, getting Firefox to shut up about its warning actually makes your code much slower and use much more memory then if firefox just silently cleared the texture on its own. Hence why I say that warning should not exist\n\nFirefox’s developers have the POV that anytime WebGL does something heavy they want to give you a warning. Given the cure makes your code more heavy I disagree with their POV. Chrome does not give this warning. It also confuses developers as they think they’re doing something wrong. They’re not doing anything wrong.\n\nhttps://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show\\_bug.cgi?id=1478216\n\nAs for things not rendering, in the code you posted you’ve put nothing in the texture so of course the texture is 0,0,0,0.\n\nThe question and quoted portions thereof are CC BY-SA 4.0 bycaka fromhere \n\nEnglishDeutsch日本語한국어Português BrasileiroРусский简体中文 \n\n* Fundamentals\n   * How to use WebGL2\n   * Fundamentals\n   * How It Works\n   * Shaders and GLSL\n   * WebGL2 State Diagram\n* WebGL2 vs WebGL1\n   * What's new in WebGL2\n   * Moving from WebGL1 to WebGL2\n   * Differences from WebGLFundamentals.org to WebGL2Fundamentals.org\n* Image Processing\n   * Image Processing\n   * Image Processing Continued\n* 2D translation, rotation, scale, matrix math\n   * 2D Translation\n   * 2D Rotation\n   * 2D Scale\n   * 2D Matrices\n* 3D\n   * Orthographic 3D\n   * 3D Perspective\n   * 3D - Cameras\n   * 3D - Matrix Naming\n* Lighting\n   * Directional Lighting\n   * Point Lighting\n   * Spot Lighting\n* Structure and Organization\n   * Less Code, More Fun\n   * Drawing Multiple Things\n   * Scene Graphs\n* Geometry\n   * 3D Geometry - Lathe\n   * Loading .obj files\n   * Loading .obj w .mtl files\n* Textures\n   * Textures\n   * Data Textures\n   * Using 2 or More Textures\n   * Cross Origin Images\n   * Perspective Correct Texture Mapping\n   * Planar and Perspective Projection Mapping\n* Rendering To A Texture\n   * Render to Texture\n* Shadows\n   * Shadows\n* Techniques\n   * 2D\n      * 2D -       "chunk": "r3fReact Three Fiber.docs\n\nSearch for anythingPress / to search\n\n# Loading Textures\n\nLet's load some fancy textures.\n\n\u003e All textures used in this chapter were downloaded from cc0textures.\n\nUsing TextureLoader and useLoader \n\nTo load the textures we will use the &#96;TextureLoader&#96; from three.js in combination with &#96;useLoader&#96; that will allow us to pass the location of the texture and get the map back.\n\nIt's better to explain with code, let's say you downloaded this texture and placed it in the public folder of your site, to get the color map from it you could do:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\nconst colorMap = useLoader(TextureLoader, 'PavingStones092_1K_Color.jpg')\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nLet's then with this information create a small scene where we can use this texture:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;jsx\nimport { Suspense } from 'react'\nimport { Canvas, useLoader } from '@react-three/fiber'\nimport { TextureLoader } from 'three'\n\nfunction Scene() {\n  const colorMap = useLoader(TextureLoader, 'PavingStones092_1K_Color.jpg')\n  return (\n    \u003c\u003e\n      \u003cambientLight intensity={0.2} /\u003e\n      \u003cdirectionalLight /\u003e\n      \u003cmesh\u003e\n        \u003csphereGeometry args={[1, 32, 32]} /\u003e\n        \u003cmeshStandardMaterial /\u003e\n      \u003c/mesh\u003e\n    \u003c/\u003e\n  )\n}\n\nexport default function App() {\n  return (\n    \u003cCanvas\u003e\n      \u003cSuspense fallback={null}\u003e\n        \u003cScene /\u003e\n      \u003c/Suspense\u003e\n    \u003c/Canvas\u003e\n  )\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIf everything went according to plan, you should now be able to apply this texture to the sphere like so:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;jsx\n\u003cmeshStandardMaterial map={colorMap} /\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nAwesome! That works but we have a lot more textures to import and do we have to create a different useLoader for each of them?\n\nThat's the great part! You don't, the second argument is an array where you can pass all the textures you have and the maps will be returned and ready to use:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\nconst [colorMap, displacementMap, normalMap, roughnessMap, aoMap] = useLoader(TextureLoader, [\n  'PavingStones092_1K_Color.jpg',\n  'PavingStones092_1K_Displacement.jpg',\n  'PavingStones092_1K_Normal.jpg',\n  'PavingStones092_1K_Roughness.jpg',\n  'PavingStones092_1K_AmbientOcclusion.jpg',\n])\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nNow we can place them in our mesh like so:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;jsx\n\u003cmeshStandardMaterial\n  map={colorMap}\n  displacementMap={displacementMap}\n  normalMap={normalMap}\n  roughnessMap={roughnessMap}\n  aoMap={aoMap}\n/\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThe displacement will probably be too much, usually setting it to 0.2 will make it look good. Our final code would look something like:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;jsx\nfunction Scene() {\n  const [colorMap, displacementMap, normalMap, roughnessMap, aoMap] = useLoader(TextureLoader, [\n    'PavingStones092_1K_Color.jpg',\n    'PavingStones092_1K_Displacement.jpg',\n    'PavingStones092_1K_Normal.jpg',\n    'PavingStones092_1K_Roughness.jpg',\n    'PavingStones092_1K_AmbientOcclusion.jpg',\n  ])\n  return (\n    \u003cmesh\u003e\n      {/* Width and height segments for displacementMap */}\n      \u003csphereGeometry args={[1, 100, 100]} /\u003e\n      \u003cmeshStandardMaterial\n        displacementScale={0.2}\n        map={colorMap}\n        displacementMap={displacementMap}\n        normalMap={normalMap}\n        roughnessMap={roughnessMap}\n        aoMap={aoMap}\n      /\u003e\n    \u003c/mesh\u003e\n  )\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nUsing useTexture \n\nAnother way to import these is using &#96;useTexture&#96; from @react-three/drei, that will make it slightly easier and there is no need to import the &#96;TextureLoader&#96;, our code would look like:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\nimport { useTexture } from \"@react-three/drei\"\n\n...\n\nconst [colorMap, displacementMap, normalMap, roughnessMap, aoMap] = useTexture([\n  'PavingStones092_1K_Color.jpg',\n  'PavingStones092_1K_Displacement.jpg',\n  'PavingStones092_1K_Normal.jpg',\n  'PavingStones092_1K_Roughness.jpg',\n  'PavingStones092_1K_AmbientOcclusion.jpg',\n])\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nYou can also use object-notation which is the most convenient:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;jsx\nconst props = useTexture({\n  map: 'PavingStones092_1K_Color.jpg',\n  displacementMap: 'PavingStones092_1K_Displacement.jpg',\n  normalMap: 'PavingStones092_1K_Normal.jpg',\n  roughnessMap: 'PavingStones092_1K_Roughness.jpg',\n  aoMap: 'PavingStones092_1K_AmbientOcclusion.jpg',\n})\n\nreturn (\n  \u003cmesh\u003e\n    \u003csphereGeometry args={[1, 32, 32]} /\u003e\n    \u003cmeshStandardMaterial {...props} /\u003e\n  \u003c/mesh\u003e\n)\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nYou can play with the sandbox and see how it looks:\n\nTextureLoader\n\n###### TextureLoader\n\nEdit this page\n\nPrevious\n\nLoading Models\n\nNext\n\nBasic Animations\n\n* getting started\n* api\n* advanced\n* tutorials  \n   * v9 Migration Guide  \n   * Events and Interaction  \n   * Loading Models  \n   * Loading Textures  \n   * Basic Animations  \n   * How does it work?\n\nOn This Page\n\n#### Using TextureLoader and useLoader\n\n#### Using useTexture",
